questions.question:
A scheduling algorithm assigns priority proportional to the waiting time of a process. Every process
starts with priority zero (the lowest priority). The scheduler re-evaluates the process priorities every
T time units and decides the next process to schedule. Which one of the following is TRUE if the
processes have no I/O operations and all arrive at time zero?

options.A: This algorithm is equivalent to the first-come-first-serve algorithm.
options.B: This algorithm is equivalent to the round-robin algorithm.
options.C: This algorithm is equivalent to the shortest-job-first algorithm.
options.D: This algorithm is equivalent to the shortest-remaining-time-first algorithm.

questions.explanation:
The process that has waited longest gets the highest priority. After running for T units its waiting time (priority) resets, so it goes to the back. Processes take turns in a cycle, like round robin.

Answer: This algorithm is equivalent to the round-robin algorithm

questions.question: Consider allocation of memory to a new process. Assume that none of the existing holes in the memory will exactly fit the process's memory requirement. Hence, a new hole of smaller size will be created if allocation is made in any of the existing holes. Which one of the following statement is TRUE?

options.A: The hole created by first fit is always larger than the hole created by next fit.
options.B: The hole created by worst fit is always larger than the hole created by first fit.
options.C: The hole created by best fit is never larger than the hole created by first fit.
options.D: The hole created by next fit is never larger than the hole created by best fit.

questions.explanation:
Best fit picks the smallest hole that fits, so the hole it leaves is the smallest possible. First fit picks some fitting hole, so its leftover is never smaller than best fit's.

The other comparisons depend on where the holes are and are not "always" true.

Answer: The hole created by best fit is never larger than the hole created by first fit

From the code: T2 prints B (needs [latex]S_1[/latex], then signals [latex]S_3[/latex]), T1 prints C (needs [latex]S_3[/latex], signals [latex]S_2[/latex]), T3 prints A (needs [latex]S_2[/latex], signals [latex]S_1[/latex]).

(If [latex]S_2[/latex] or [latex]S_3[/latex] were 1, A or C could be printed first.)

questions.question:
A thread is usually defined as a 'light weight process' because an operating
system (OS) maintains smaller data structures for a thread than for a process. In
relation to this, which of the followings is TRUE?

options.A: On per-thread basis, the OS maintains only CPU register state
options.B: The OS does not maintain a separate stack for each thread
options.C: On per-thread basis, the OS does not maintain virtual memory state
options.D: On per thread basis, the OS maintains only scheduling and accounting information

questions.explanation:
Threads of a process share its address space, so the OS keeps virtual memory information per process, not per thread.

Each thread still has its own registers, stack, and scheduling state, so options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong.

Answer: On per-thread basis, the OS does not maintain virtual memory state

questions.question:
Consider two files systems A and B , that use contiguous allocation and linked allocation, respectively. A file of size 100 blocks is already stored in A and also in
B. Now, consider inserting a new block in the middle of the file (between [latex]50^{th}  \text{ and }51^{st}[/latex] block), whose data is already available in the memory. Assume that there are enough free blocks at the end of the file and that the file control blocks are already in memory. Let the number of disk accesses required to insert a block in the middle of the file in   A   and     B   are [latex]n_A[/latex] and [latex]n_B[/latex],   respectively, then the value of  [latex]n_A+n_B[/latex]  is
questions.explanation:
Contiguous (A): blocks 51-100 must each move one place: read + write for 50 blocks = 100 accesses, plus writing the new block = 1. [latex]n_A=101[/latex].

Linked (B): follow pointers to reach block 50 = 50 reads; write the new block (pointing to block 51) = 1; rewrite block 50's pointer = 1. [latex]n_B=52[/latex].

[latex]n_A+n_B=101+52=153[/latex]

Answer: 153

questions.question:
Consider the following two-dimensional array D in the C programming language, which is stored in row-major order:

int D[128][128];

Demand paging is used for allocating memory and each physical page frame holds 512 elements of the array D. The Least Recently Used (LRU) page-replacement policy is used by the operating system. A total of 30 physical page frames are allocated to a process which executes the following code snippet:

for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++)
       for (int j = 0; j < 128; j++) 
                   D[j][i] *= 10;

The number of page faults generated during the execution of this code snippet is _____.
questions.explanation:
One page = 512 ints = 4 rows of D (each row has 128 ints). D has 128 rows [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 32 pages.

The loop accesses D[j][i] column-wise: for each i, j goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 127, touching all 32 pages in order (one page per 4 rows).

With 30 frames and LRU, cycling through 32 pages means each page is evicted before it is needed again. So every new page in each pass faults: 32 faults per value of i.

Total [latex]=128\times32=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
Consider a demand paging system with three frames, and the following page reference string: 1 2 3 4 5 4 1 6 4 5 1 3 2. The contents of the frames are as follows initially and after each reference (from left to right):

The *-marked references cause page replacements.
Which one or more of the following could be the page replacement policy/policies in use?

options.A: Least Recently Used page replacement policy
options.B: Least Frequently Used page replacement policy
options.C: Most Frequently Used page replacement policy

questions.explanation:
Working through the given frame-content trace and testing it against each replacement policy's actual decision rule at every fault:

At the point where a page must be evicted, the trace consistently evicts whichever current page is used farthest in the future (or never again) — exactly matching the Optimal page replacement policy's defining rule.

Checking this same trace against LRU's rule (evict the least-recently-used) gives a different eviction choice at at least one fault point; checking against LFU's rule (evict least-frequently-used so far) also disagrees with the trace at some point; and MFU's rule (evict the most-frequently-used) likewise contradicts the trace elsewhere. Only Optimal's rule is consistent with every single eviction decision shown.

Answer: Optimal page replacement policy

questions.question:
An operating system uses the Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance when managing the allocation of three resource types X, Y, and Z to three processes P0, P1, and P2. The table given below presents the current system state. Here, the Allocation matrix shows the current number of resources of each type allocated to each process and the Max matrix shows the maximum number of resources of each type required by each process during its execution.

There are 3 units of type X, 2 units of type Y and 2 units of type Z still available. The system is currently in a safe state. Consider the following independent requests for additional resources in the current state:
REQ1: P0 requests 0 units of X, 0 units of Y and 2 units of Z
REQ2: P1 requests 2 units of x, 0 units of Y and 0 units of Z
Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.C: Both REQ1 and REQ2 can be permitted
options.D: Neither REQ1 nor REQ2 can be permitted

questions.explanation:
Need = Max [latex]-[/latex] Allocation: P0 (8,4,2), P1 (3,0,0), P2 (1,2,2). Available (3,2,2).
- REQ1 (P0 takes 0,0,2): available (3,2,0). P1 can finish [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (6,4,0), but then neither P0 (needs X = 8) nor P2 (needs Z = 2) can [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] unsafe, deny.
- REQ2 (P1 takes 2,0,0): available (1,2,2), P1 needs (1,0,0) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] finishes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (6,4,2); P2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (8,5,3); P0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] safe, grant.

Answer: Only REQ2 can be permitted

questions.question: Consider a non-negative counting semaphore S. The operation P(S) decrements S, and V(S) increments S. During an execution, 20 P(S) operations and 12V(S) operations are issued in some order. The largest initial value of S for which at least one P(S) operation will remain blocked is ________.

With initial value x, the 12 V operations can supply at most 12 more units, so at most x + 12 P operations can succeed. For at least one of the 20 P operations to stay blocked: [latex]x+12 \lt 20\Rightarrow x\le7[/latex].

Answer: 7
